title: Person or Setting? Workplace Explanation Laboratory
summary: Evidence about one fictional team arrives in three rounds, and you commit to an explanation after each. Then spend a budget across three levels and see what your combination leaves in force.
learningObjectives: Construct individual, relational and organisational explanations of the same workplace problem.
Explain why a real, replicable difference between people does not locate its own cause.
State what each intervention targets and precisely what it leaves in place.
Judge the limits of a matched-team comparison that was matched at recruitment and is not matched now.
Resist both the claim that psychological intervention is a distraction and the claim that structural explanation always wins.
interactionTypes: staged evidence release with a recorded answer trail
costed intervention selection against a budget
bar chart with full text equivalent
privacy: Every selection is held in the browser tab only and discarded when the page is left; nothing is saved, stored or transmitted, and no score or judgement about the person using it is produced.
accessibilityNotes: Nothing is timed. All controls are native radios, checkboxes and buttons in labelled fieldsets, and committing with nothing selected produces an explanatory message that treats 'several at once' as a real answer. Evidence released in later rounds carries a heavier left rule, but each item states its own number and the round heading names what has just arrived, so nothing is carried by the rule alone. Interventions the remaining budget cannot cover are disabled, dimmed, and say so in their own cost line rather than relying on opacity. The outcome chart is hidden from assistive technology and paired with a sentence giving the before and after scores, the comparison team, the projected leavers and the cost; every value is also printed beside its own bar. Both experiments announce every change through the shell's polite live region, and either reset button restores the entire page including the prediction gate and the other experiment. Headings run h1 to h5 without skipping, focus moves to the first experiment's heading when the gate opens, the stage track carries aria-current with a done state in text, targets are at least 2.75rem, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: A correlation of 0.61 inside one team, a rota that is the same for all fourteen, and a budget that covers half of what is needed
simulationNotes: Kelbridge Service Centre, its two teams, its review, its exhaustion scale and all its figures were written for this page; no real organisation, team, incident, instrument or person is described, and no number is a norm, a prevalence or a published effect. Nothing is random. Experiment 1 releases four individual-level items, then three relational items, then four items about the work including a comparison team at 38 against Team B's 74; the explanation feedback differs by round and by answer, and round 1 treats the individual-level answer as the best-supported reading of the evidence available, because it is. Experiment 2 starts at a team mean of 74 on a 0-100 scale with three projected leavers of fourteen, and subtracts: resilience workshops 6 (halved to 3 when nothing structural is also chosen, because the conditions reload what the training discharged), coaching for two 1, weekly protected debrief 9, supervisor feedback practice 8, rota and recovery redesign 18, target and discretion change 16, with a further 3 for taking the two relational changes together and a further 5 for taking the two structural changes together. Costs are 2, 2, 3, 3, 5 and 5 against a budget of 10, so the six together (20 units) are unreachable by design. Projected leavers are round(3 x (after / 74) ^ 1.6). The two ten-unit extremes reach 50 (everything individual and relational) and 35 (the two structural changes alone). That the structural combination outperforms is true by construction and is stated as such on the page; the evidence about what works in real workplaces is in the literature, not here.
